title: CuTe DSL Limitations Overview
critical_patterns: Use conditional logic instead of early exits in loops
Define variables before control flow blocks to access them outside
Maintain type stability; use different variables for different types
Use assertions instead of exceptions in dynamic control flow
Use range() for runtime values and range_constexpr() for compile-time constants
Allocate memory in host code and pass to kernels
Manually handle broadcasting in kernel logic
constraints: No early exit from loops (break, continue, return)
Variables defined in control flow are not available outside
Cannot change variable types in control flow
No exceptions in dynamic control flow
Cannot mix compile-time and runtime values
Limited Python object support in kernels
No dynamic memory allocation in kernels
Limited type inference; explicit annotation may be needed
Shared memory limits per block vary by architecture
Maximum threads per block and grid dimensions are architecture dependent
Limited Python debugging tools in kernels
JIT compilation overhead on first call
Not supported in kernels: classes, OOP, generators, async/await, context managers, decorators, lambda functions, list/dict comprehensions
compressed_summary: CuTe DSL is designed with specific limitations to ensure safety, predictability, and performance. Understanding these constraints is crucial for writing effective GPU kernels. Dynamic control flow limitations include no early exits from loops and the isolation of variables defined within control blocks. Compile-time and runtime values must not be mixed, and dynamic memory allocation is not supported within kernels. The type system requires stability, with no automatic broadcasting of operations. Preprocessor mode, when set to False, introduces severe limitations such as branch collapse and loop unrolling. Architecture-specific constraints include shared memory limits and tensor core requirements. Threading and synchronization are subject to architecture-dependent limits on block and grid sizes. Debugging within kernels is limited, with standard Python tools being ineffective; instead, use cute.printf() and logging. Performance considerations include JIT compilation overhead and potential slowdowns with dynamic shapes. Language features such as classes, OOP, and async/await are not supported within kernels. Best practices involve starting simple, using default settings, validating early, profiling before optimization, and carefully reading error messages. When encountering limitations, consult documentation, simplify code, seek help, or consider alternative approaches like raw CUDA or Triton.
